label: Investigation of the Equations of Motion
notes: This chapter leaves general theory and asks a concrete question: for a system with one degree of freedom, what does every trajectory look like without solving the differential equation. The answer is qualitative geometry on the phase plane, where conserved energy organizes all motion into level curves.

label: One Degree of Freedom
notes: We fix the simplest non-trivial setting: a single coordinate moving under a force derived from a potential. Newton's law becomes a first-order vector field on the phase plane of position and velocity, and that field is what we will read off without any explicit integration.

label: The Phase Plane
notes: Velocity and acceleration define a planar vector field whose integral curves are the phase curves. Through each point passes exactly one curve, so the plane foliates into disjoint trajectories. Equilibria sit where the field vanishes, and the picture of all curves is the phase portrait we want.

label: Conservation of Energy
notes: Multiplying the equation of motion by velocity and integrating reveals a conserved quantity, the total energy. This is the central invariant of the chapter: kinetic plus potential energy stays constant along motion, so each phase curve lies inside a single level set of the energy function.

label: Phase Curves as Energy Levels
notes: Because energy is conserved, the phase curves are exactly the connected components of the level sets E equals constant. The motion in a potential well becomes a problem of slicing the energy surface horizontally and reading the resulting curves, which is pure one-variable calculus made geometric.

label: Potential Wells and Phase Portrait
notes: Place the potential graph above the phase plane and slide an energy line across it. Inside a well the level set closes into an oval of periodic motion; at a maximum the curves cross in a saddle. The shape of the potential dictates every qualitative feature of the portrait below.

label: Equilibria and Stability
notes: Critical points of the potential are equilibria. A strict minimum gives a center surrounded by closed orbits and is Lyapunov stable; a maximum gives a saddle and is unstable. Linearizing the field at the equilibrium recovers these types from the sign of the second derivative of the potential.

label: The Period of Oscillation
notes: For motion trapped in a well between two turning points, the time of one full oscillation is an explicit integral of one over the velocity. The velocity follows from energy conservation, so the period is computed directly from the potential without ever solving the equation of motion.

label: The Pendulum and Separatrices
notes: The pendulum unites every phenomenon: small oscillations near the bottom, rotations over the top, and the dividing curve between them. That separatrix passes through the unstable upright saddle, takes infinite time to traverse, and cleanly partitions the cylinder of states into libration and rotation.

label: Central Force Fields
notes: We move to the plane and consider forces pointing along the radius with magnitude depending only on distance. Angular momentum is conserved because there is no tangential force, and this single invariant lets us eliminate the angle and reduce the planar motion to one radial degree of freedom.

label: The Effective Potential
notes: After fixing angular momentum, the radial coordinate moves in an effective potential that adds a centrifugal barrier to the true potential. The chapter's one-degree-of-freedom machinery now applies verbatim: energy levels on this effective curve dictate bounded orbits, unbounded escape, and circular motion.

label: Kepler's Problem
notes: For the inverse-square attraction the orbit equation integrates to a conic section, with energy fixing whether it is an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola. Bounded negative-energy orbits are ellipses, recovering Kepler's first law and closing the chapter on a fully solved, historically decisive example.
